title: Haiku 5.5 matches Sonnet 5.5 on retrieval. It costs a fifth as much.
summary: We ran Haiku 4.5, Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 at every effort level on 18 real retrieval questions and 10 real filing jobs, scored by a blind judge. Haiku…
body_markdown:
**Research note**


**71.7%** vs **71.3%** on retrieval


**4.8×** the cost for Sonnet


**223** graded runs


9 Oct 2026


**One question, two models, replayed from the real traces.** Haiku 5.5 at medium effort (left) and Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort (right) answer the same retrieval question. Folders light up as each agent opens them. Haiku finds more and costs $0.45. Sonnet sends 5 readers and costs $4.34. Folder and fact names are made generic. Section 6 has the details. The short version


- **Haiku 5.5 finds what Sonnet 5.5 finds, for much less.** On the 6 retrieval questions every setup ran, Haiku 5.5 at high effort scores 71.7% at $1.15 per attempt. Sonnet 5.5 at high effort scores 71.3% at $5.57: 4.8× the cost.
- **Haiku 5.5 at extra high effort scores above Sonnet 5.5 at medium and high.** 73.6% against 70.9% and 71.3%, on the same 6 questions.
- **Over all 18 questions, Sonnet keeps a lead.** Haiku 5.5 medium scores 68.8% at $0.37. Sonnet 5.5 medium scores 74.5% at $2.30, 6.2× the cost.
- **Filing is close too.** Haiku 5.5 high scores 69.1% at $1.47 per job. Sonnet 5.5 medium scores 71.9% at $5.20, 3.5× the cost.
- **More effort can score less.** Haiku 5.5 scores less at high than at medium on retrieval, and less at extra high than at high on filing. One run of one question can move by 6 points. Averaged over our 6 questions, a gap under 4 points is within noise.
- **Haiku 4.5 is far behind.** 43.9% on retrieval over 18 questions, at twice the cost of Haiku 5.5 medium.
- **We are switching.** Our retrieval agent moves to Haiku 5.5 at medium effort, our filing agent to Haiku 5.5 at high effort, with filing still under a check.


## 1


What we tested, from zero


Every answer our AI assistant gives about our own company starts with a search. It reads our notes, our past projects and our playbooks before it writes a word. After the work is done, another agent files what was learned. Those two jobs run all day. They were running on Sonnet. We wanted to know if a smaller model could do them as well.


### Two jobs we gave the models


- **Retrieval.** A request comes in, such as "what do we know about this client's tender process?". A **retrieval agent** plans the search, reads the files and writes a short report of what it found, with sources.
- **Filing.** A working session ends. A **filing agent** reads what happened and writes the lasting lessons into the right place: private company notes, or a shared copy with every client detail removed.


### Agents, subagents and readers


**An agent is a model with instructions and tools.** It can read files, run searches and start other agents. An agent started by another agent is a **subagent** .


For a wide question, our retrieval agent splits the search. It starts **reader subagents** , one per area, and merges what they send back. A filing agent also starts a reader first, to see what is already filed. More readers means more coverage, and more cost.


### Effort


**Effort is a setting that tells the model how much to think before it acts.** Claude models take five levels: low, medium, high, extra high and max. Higher effort uses more tokens, so it costs more. It also changes how the agent works: at higher effort it tends to start more readers and run more searches.


### The three models


- **Haiku 4.5.** The small Claude model we tried before. It has no effort setting.
- **Haiku 5.5.** The new small model.
- **Sonnet 5.5.** The mid sized model. Our agents ran on Sonnet until now.


### How a score works


**Each question has an answer key: the facts a good answer must contain.** A blind judge reads each answer and marks every fact found, half found or missed. The score is the share of the key the answer earned. 72% means 72% of the facts.


**Finding** Both jobs run on every company question we ask. A cheaper model that scores the same cuts the cost of every answer.


## 2


How we tested


We built the test from our own work, then paid for every model and effort level to run it. Here is the whole method, in the order it ran.


1. **Collect.** Take real requests from our own past work.
2. **Key.** Write the facts a good answer must hold, and check each one against its source.
3. **Copy.** Give every run its own fenced copy of our knowledge workspaces.
4. **Pin.** Set one model and one effort level for every agent in the run.
5. **Run.** Start the agent with the original request, word for word.
6. **Verify.** Read every agent's transcript and confirm the model and effort it ran on.
7. **Judge.** A blind judge scores each answer against its key.
8. **Compare.** Average score and cost per setup, on the same questions.


### The two jobs


- **Retrieval.** The retrieval agent reads the request and plans the search. For a wide question it starts reader subagents, one per area of our workspaces. Each reader searches its area and reports back. The retrieval agent merges what they found and writes a report with a source for every fact.
- **Filing.** The filing agent reads a finished working session. It first starts a reader to see what is already filed. It writes private company notes itself. Then it can start three filers, one per shared library: tools, team patterns and use cases. Each filer writes a shared copy with every client detail removed.


### Where the tasks came from


- **18 retrieval questions.** Each is a real request our retrieval agent answered in the six weeks before the test. They cover a contact's details, a brand canon for a new site, past decisions behind a proposal, how a client runs a tender, our own positioning, and similar company questions.
- **Answer keys checked against their sources.** We started from the original answer and any later correction from the person who asked. A reader then opened every source file. A fact no source confirmed was dropped. Each key holds 4 to 12 facts, 196 in all.
- **Partial credit.** A found fact counts 1, a half found fact 0.5, a missed fact 0. The score is the mean over the key.
- **Facts outside the workspaces, scored apart.** 17 of the live only in our CRM, a mailbox or a local file. The fence blocks those, so they sit in a separate column and stay out of every chart.
- **5 questions excluded.** Their answers live in another organisation's workspace, which was outside the copy. No setup could have found them. We replaced them with 5 reserve questions from the same pool.
- **10 filing jobs.** Each comes from a real working session, cut at the moment the filing agent was first started. Its key lists what must be filed, where it must go, and what must never appear, such as a secret or a client name in a shared copy. Two jobs should file nothing, to test restraint.


### The workspace copy


- **4 drives, 8,943 files:** company notes (6,463), tools (809), team patterns (1,534) and use cases (137).
- **A fresh copy per run.** Every run started from the same snapshot, so no run could see another run's writes.
- **A fence.** A guard checked every command an agent ran. It blocked our live workspaces, the CRM, the mailbox, other organisations and any write outside the run's own folder. We also compared the live workspaces before and after each run. No real data could change.
- **Filing starts before the original filing.** For each job, we rolled the copy back to the moment the original filing agent started. Files it created were removed. Files it changed were rolled back to their earlier text, as closely as the workspace history allowed. The agent then saw only what existed at that moment.


### Pinning the model and the effort


- **One definition per setup.** Each setup got its own copy of the agent instructions. Only the model line and the effort line differ. A diff over all 11 setups found no other change.
- **Subagents inherit.** When an agent starts another, the guard removes any model or effort it asks for. Every subagent runs on the setup's model and effort.
- **Checked after the run.** A script read every agent's transcript and confirmed the model and effort it ran on. A run that failed this check was not graded.


### The 11 setups


Table 1 · The 11 setups Setup Model Effort Retrieval questions graded Filing jobs graded


Haiku 4.5 claude-haiku-4-5 none (no effort setting) 18 10


Haiku 5.5, five levels claude-haiku-5-5 low, medium, high, extra high, max 18 each; max 2 10 each; max 4

Haiku 4.5 has no effort control, so it runs once, as it comes.


### The blind judge


- **The judge.** claude-opus-5-5 at high effort, with no tools and no project settings.
- **What it saw.** The answer, or the files a filing run wrote, and the key. Model names, effort words, run names and agent names were removed first.
- **The rubric.** Each fact in the key is found, half found or missed. For filing, a fact filed in the wrong place keeps its credit and costs a fixed 0.25 once, for placement. A job that should file nothing scores 1 when nothing is filed, else 0.
- **Consistency.** We gave the judge the same answer twice, on two cells. Each time one fact moved from half found to found. Each cell moved by 0.045, under 0.05.
- **A human read.** A person on our team reviewed 10 graded answers, chosen to cover close calls, a zero, a perfect score and a job that should file nothing, and found no grade to change.


### Why some points use a shared sample


The costly setups could not run every question inside our usage limits. Sonnet 5.5 at high, extra high and max, and Haiku 5.5 at max, ran out first. So the retrieval chart compares every setup on the same **shared sample of 6 questions** that all eight of them finished. Section 3 then shows the 7 setups that finished all 18.


### Run to run variance


One run per question can swing. So we ran Sonnet 5.5 low and medium 3 times on each of the 6 shared questions. Section 5 has the result.


### Cost


- **Billed cost per run.** Each run reports what it cost, including every subagent it started. Two cells had no billed figure, so we used the list price of their tokens.
- **The judge is counted apart.** Section 9 lists it.


### What failed


We started 477 runs for the 11 setups. 223 were graded. 237 were cut: by usage limits, outages, a failed model check, budget caps, or agents still working when the run closed. 14 repeated a question already graded, and 3 filing runs started from the wrong state. None of these was scored. 7 filing jobs at Sonnet 5.5 max effort never ran.

### Sonnet 5.5 at max effort


We started 25 retrieval runs of Sonnet 5.5 at max effort. Every one was cut by a usage limit, an outage or a time limit before it closed. So max effort was not graded, and every cost below is a partial cost: a lower bound. The runs still show how the agent behaves.


- **In 13 of the 25 runs, the retrieval agent started 8 readers.**
- **Those 13 runs cost each at the median** and $16.02 on average, at list price, up to $23.75. These are lower bounds. A finished run would have cost more.
- **The cost is real reading.** In the three runs we traced, each of the 8 readers was started once and made 9 to 90 tool calls in its own area. No reader was restarted.


**Finding** At max effort, Sonnet 5.5 spends more on one question than Haiku 5.5 medium spends on all 18 together. Wide search has a price. Set the effort level per job, and cap the number of readers.


## 8


A defect the test found


Reading the answers turned up a defect in our own retrieval agent. It is a fault in how the agent waits, and it hides real quality.


- **What happened.** The agent started its readers, then wrote its report before their results came back. Every need in the report read "pending".
- **How we counted.** A graded run counts when at least half of the needs in its report read "pending" and the judge scored it 0.
- **How often.** 3 graded runs: 2 at Haiku 5.5 high; 1 at Haiku 5.5 extra high. Each started 3 or 5 readers. Each scored 0.
- **Why it matters.** The readers did the work and the answer dropped it. Those zeros pull down the Haiku 5.5 high and extra high averages in sections 3 and 5.
- **What we do about it.** The agent must wait for every reader it started before it writes. That is an instruction change, and it applies to every model.


**Finding** Read the answers as well as the scores. A score of 0 can mean the model failed, or the agent around it failed. Here it was the agent.

## 10


What we are changing


We are moving both agents to Haiku 5.5.


Table 8 · What we are changing, and why Agent Before From now Why


Retrieval agent and its readers Sonnet Haiku 5.5, medium effort 68.8% against 74.5% over 18 questions, at 1/6.2 the cost per attempt


Filing agent Sonnet Haiku 5.5, high effort, under a check 69.1% against 71.9% over 10 jobs, at 1/3.5 the cost; its score swings with effort, so we keep checking what it files


Haiku 4.5 anywhere Not used Not used 43.9% on retrieval over 18 questions, the lowest of every model we tried


Three rules we take from this:


- **Test the small model on your own work.** The model sheet does not tell you this. Haiku 5.5 matched Sonnet 5.5 on our shared sample and came within 5.7 points on the full set.
- **Pick effort per job.** Medium suits our retrieval. High suits our filing. Extra high cost more, scored within the noise of medium on retrieval and lower on filing.
- **Read the answers.** Three zeros in our data came from the agent, and the model was blameless.


## 11


The fine print


- **Small sets.** 18 retrieval questions and 10 filing jobs. Section 5 shows how much one question can swing.
- **One judge.** Every score comes from one blind judge, claude-opus-5-5. It moved one fact per cell when asked twice.
- **Single runs.** Each cell is one run, except the variance study on Sonnet 5.5 low and medium.
- **Our own tasks.** The questions and jobs come from our own work and our own knowledge workspaces. Yours will differ.
- **Partial grids.** Sonnet 5.5 high, extra high and max, and Haiku 5.5 max, did not finish every task. Their points use the shared sample, or are left out.
- **Facts outside the workspaces.** CRM and mailbox facts were fenced off and excluded from every score here.
- **We run these agents.** They search and file our own knowledge every day. That is a stake in the result, so read the conclusions with it in mind.
- **Our setup favours the incumbent.** The agent instructions were written and tuned while the agents ran on Sonnet. Haiku ran them unchanged.
- **Cost is per run, as reported.** Each run's own billed total, with its subagents. Two cells use the list price of their tokens.
- **Dates.** The runs and grading took place on 7 and 8 October 2026.


## 12


Glossary


AgentA model with instructions and tools. It can read files, run searches and start other agents.Answer keyThe facts a good answer must contain, written before any model ran.Blind judgeA model that scores each answer without knowing which model or effort level wrote it.Bootstrap intervalA range found by resampling the measured runs many times. The true value probably sits inside it.Cost per attemptWhat one run of one question or job cost, including every subagent it started.EffortA setting that tells the model how much to think before it acts: low, medium, high, extra high or max.FenceThe guard that kept every run inside its own copy of our data.Filing agentThe agent that writes what a working session taught us into the right workspace.Partial creditA found fact counts 1, a half found fact 0.5, a missed fact 0.Reader subagentA subagent the retrieval agent starts to search one area and report back.Retrieval agentThe agent that plans a search across our workspaces and writes a report with sources.Run to run noiseHow much the score of the same setup on the same question moves between runs.Shared sampleThe 6 retrieval questions every setup finished, used to compare them fairly.SubagentAn agent started by another agent.TokenA small piece of text, a few characters long. Models are billed per token.WorkspaceA shared drive of files that holds our company knowledge.
